And indeed, if it is true, as I think I have proved, that he must have lived many ages before he could either desire or have the opportunity of escaping that state, this would only be an accusation against nature, and not against the being she had thus unhappily constituted. But as I understand the word miserable, it either has no meaning at all or means only the painful privation of something, or a state of suffering in body or soul. I would be glad to have explained to me what kind of misery a free being can possibly suffer whose heart is at ease and whose body is in health. I would ask also whether a social or a natural life is more likely to become unbearable to those who enjoy it. We see around us hardly a creature in civil society who does not lament his existence; we even see many deprive themselves of as much of it as they can, and human and divine laws combined can hardly stop the disorder. Has it ever been known that a savage at liberty took it into his head to complain of life or to make away with himself? Let us judge, then, with less vanity, on which side the real misery lies. On the other hand, nothing could be more unhappy than savage man dazzled by science, tormented by his passions, and reasoning about a state different from his own. It appears that Providence most wisely arranged that the faculties he potentially possessed should develop only as occasion offered to exercise them, so that they would not be superfluous or burdensome to him by appearing before their time, nor slow and useless when the need for them arose. In instinct alone he had everything he needed for living in the state of nature; and with a developed understanding he has only just enough to support life in society.

It appears, at first glance, that men in a state of nature, having no moral relations or determinate obligations with one another, could not be either good or bad, virtuous or vicious—unless we take these terms in a physical sense, and call vices, in an individual, those qualities that may injure his preservation, and virtues those that contribute to it; in which case the most virtuous would be the one who put least check on the pure impulses of nature. But without deviating from the ordinary sense of the words, it will be proper to suspend the judgment we might be led to form about such a state and to guard ourselves against our prejudices, until we have weighed the matter in the scales of impartiality and seen whether virtues or vices preponderate among civilized men, and whether their virtues do them more good than their vices do harm; until we have discovered whether the progress of the sciences sufficiently compensates them for the harm they do one another in proportion as they are better informed of the good they ought to do; or whether they would not, on the whole, be in a much happier condition if they had nothing to fear or to hope from anyone than as they are, subjected to universal dependence and obliged to take everything from those who undertake to give them nothing in return.

Above all, let us not conclude, with Hobbes, that because man has no idea of goodness, he must be naturally wicked; that he is vicious because he doesn't know virtue; that he always refuses to do his fellow creatures services he doesn't think they have a right to demand; or that by virtue of the right he rightly claims to everything he needs, he foolishly imagines himself the sole proprietor of the whole universe. Hobbes had seen clearly the defects of all the modern definitions of natural right; but the consequences he draws from his own show that he understands it in an equally false sense. Reasoning on the principles he lays down, he ought to have said that the state of nature, being the one in which the care for our own preservation is least prejudicial to that of others, was consequently best calculated to promote peace, and the most suitable for mankind. He says the exact opposite, because he has improperly included, as part of savage man's care for his self-preservation, the gratification of a multitude of passions that are the work of society and have made laws necessary. A bad man, he says, is a robust child. But it remains to be proved that man in a state of nature is this robust child; and even if we granted that he is, what would he infer? Why, truly, that if this man, when robust and strong, were dependent on others as he is when feeble, there is no extravagance he would not be guilty of: that he would beat his mother when she was too slow in giving him her breast; that he would strangle one of his younger brothers if he found him troublesome; or that he would bite another's arm if he caused him any inconvenience. But that man in the state of nature is both strong and dependent involves two contrary suppositions. Man is weak when he is dependent, and is his own master before he comes to be strong. Hobbes did not reflect that the same cause that prevents a savage from making use of his reason (as our jurists hold) prevents him also from abusing his faculties (as Hobbes himself allows). So it may be justly said that savages are not bad merely because they don't know what it is to be good: for it is neither the development of the understanding nor the restraint of law that hinders them from doing ill, but the peacefulness of their passions and their ignorance of vice—"so much more does the ignorance of vice profit the one sort than the knowledge of virtue the other." There is another principle that escaped Hobbes, which, having been bestowed on mankind to moderate, on certain occasions, the impetuosity of egoism, or, before its birth, the desire of self-preservation, tempers the ardor with which he pursues his own welfare by an innate repugnance at seeing a fellow creature suffer. I do not think I need fear contradiction in holding that man is endowed with the only natural virtue that not even the most violent detractor of human virtue could deny him. I am speaking of compassion, a disposition suited to creatures as weak and subject to so many ills as we certainly are—all the more universal and useful to mankind because it comes before any kind of reflection, and at the same time so natural that the very beasts themselves sometimes give clear proofs of it. Not to mention the tenderness of mothers for their young and the perils they brave to save them from danger, it is well known that horses are reluctant to trample on living bodies; one animal never passes by the dead body of another of its species; there are even some that give their fellows a sort of burial; and the mournful lowing of cattle as they enter the slaughterhouse shows the impressions made on them by the horrible spectacle that meets them. We find, with pleasure, the author of the Fable of the Bees obliged to admit that man is a compassionate and sensitive being, and laying aside his cold subtle style, in the example he gives, to present us with the pathetic description of a man who, from a place of confinement, is forced to behold a wild beast tear a child from the arms of its mother, crushing its tender limbs with its murderous teeth, and tearing its quivering entrails with its claws. What horrid agitation must not the eyewitness of such a scene experience, even though he were not personally involved! What anxiety would he not suffer at not being able to give any help to the fainting mother and the dying infant!

Such is the pure emotion of nature, prior to all reflection! Such is the force of natural compassion, which the greatest depravity of morals has so far hardly been able to destroy! For every day at our theaters we see men moved—even brought to tears—by the sufferings of a wretch who, were he in the tyrant's place, would probably even add to the torments of his enemies; like the bloodthirsty Sulla, who was so sensitive to ills he had not caused, or that Alexander of Pherae who didn't dare go and see any tragedy performed, for fear of being seen weeping with Andromache and Priam, though he could listen without emotion to the cries of all the citizens who were daily strangled at his command.
"Nature avows she gave the human race the softest hearts, who gave them tears." (Juvenal, Satire xv, 151.)

Mandeville well knew that, despite all their morality, men would never have been any better than monsters had nature not bestowed on them a sense of compassion to assist their reason. But he did not see that from this quality alone flow all those social virtues he denied man any possession of. For what is generosity, clemency, or humanity but compassion applied to the weak, the guilty, or to mankind in general? Even benevolence and friendship, if we judge rightly, are only the effects of compassion constantly directed at a particular object: for how is it different to wish that another person should not suffer pain and uneasiness, and to wish him happy? Even if it were true that pity is no more than a feeling that puts us in the place of the sufferer—a feeling obscure yet lively in a savage, developed yet feeble in civilized man—this truth would have no other consequence than to confirm my argument. Compassion must, in fact, be the stronger the more the animal beholding any kind of distress identifies himself with the animal that suffers. Now, it is plain that such identification must have been much more complete in a state of nature than in a state of reason. It is reason that generates self-respect, and reflection that confirms it. It is reason that turns the human mind back on itself and divides him from everything that could disturb or afflict him. It is philosophy that isolates him and bids him say, at the sight of the misfortunes of others, "Perish if you will, I am safe." Nothing but such general evils as threaten the whole community can disturb the tranquil sleep of the philosopher or tear him from his bed. A murder may be committed under his window with impunity; he has only to put his hands over his ears and argue a little with himself to prevent nature, which is shocked within him, from identifying itself with the unfortunate sufferer. Uncivilized man has no such admirable talent, and for lack of reason and wisdom is always foolishly ready to obey the first promptings of humanity. It is the populace that crowds together at riots and street brawls, while the wise man prudently makes off. It is the mob and the market women who part the combatants, and prevent gentlefolk from cutting each other's throats.

It is therefore certain that compassion is a natural feeling that, by moderating the violence of love of self in each individual, contributes to the preservation of the whole species. It is this compassion that hurries us, without reflection, to the relief of those in distress; it is this that, in a state of nature, takes the place of laws, morals, and virtues, with the advantage that no one is tempted to disobey its gentle voice; it is this that will always prevent a strong savage from robbing a weak child or a feeble old man of the sustenance they may have acquired with pain and difficulty, so long as he sees a way of providing for himself by other means; it is this that, instead of inculcating the sublime maxim of rational justice, "Do unto others as you would have them do unto you," inspires all men with that other maxim of natural goodness—much less perfect indeed, but perhaps more useful: "Do good to yourself with as little harm as possible to others." In short, it is in this natural feeling rather than in any subtle arguments that we must look for the cause of that aversion every man would feel toward doing evil, even independently of the maxims of education. Although it might belong to Socrates and other minds of the same craft to acquire virtue by reason, the human race would long since have ceased to exist if its preservation had depended only on the reasonings of the individuals who composed it.

With passions so little active, and so good a check on them, men, being rather wild than wicked and more intent on guarding themselves against the harm that might be done to them than on doing harm to others, were by no means subject to very dangerous dissensions. They had no kind of dealings with one another, and were consequently strangers to vanity, deference, esteem, and contempt. They had not the least idea of mine and thine, and no true conception of justice. They looked on every act of violence they were subjected to as an injury easily repaired, rather than as a crime deserving punishment, and they never thought of taking revenge unless perhaps mechanically and on the spot, as a dog will sometimes bite the stone thrown at him. Their quarrels would therefore seldom have very bloody consequences, since the subject of them would be merely a question of subsistence. But I am aware of one greater danger, which remains to be noticed.

Among the passions that stir the human heart, there is one that makes the sexes necessary to each other, and is extremely ardent and impetuous—a terrible passion that braves danger, surmounts all obstacles, and in its transports seems designed to bring destruction on the very human race it is actually meant to preserve. What must become of men left to this brutal and boundless rage, without modesty, without shame, and daily defending their loves at the price of their blood?

It must, first of all, be admitted that the more violent the passions are, the more necessary laws become to keep them in check. But setting aside the inadequacy of laws to achieve this purpose—which is obvious from the crimes and disorders these passions daily give rise to among us—we should do well to inquire whether these evils did not spring up along with the laws themselves. For in that case, even if the laws were capable of suppressing such evils, the least that could be expected of them would be to check a mischief that would not have arisen without them.

Let us begin by distinguishing the physical and moral ingredients in the feeling of love. The physical part of love is that general desire that drives the sexes to unite with each other. The moral part is what determines and fixes this desire exclusively on one particular object, or at least gives it a greater degree of energy toward the object thus preferred. It is easy to see that the moral part of love is an artificial feeling, born of social custom and enhanced by women with much care and cleverness to establish their empire and put in power the sex that ought to obey. This feeling, being founded on certain ideas of beauty and merit that a savage is not in a position to acquire, and on comparisons he is incapable of making, must for him be almost nonexistent; for as his mind cannot form abstract ideas of proportion and regularity, his heart is not susceptible to the feelings of love and admiration that are imperceptibly produced by the application of these ideas. He follows solely the character nature has implanted in him, and not tastes he could never have acquired, so that every woman equally answers his purpose.

Men in a state of nature, confined merely to what is physical in love, and fortunate enough to be ignorant of those refinements that whet the appetite while increasing the difficulty of gratifying it, must be subject to fewer and less violent fits of passion, and consequently fall into fewer and less violent disputes. The imagination, which causes such ravages among us, never speaks to the heart of savages, who quietly await the impulses of nature, yield to them involuntarily, with more pleasure than ardor, and, their needs once satisfied, lose the desire. It is therefore beyond dispute that love, like all other passions, must have acquired in society the glowing impetuosity that makes it so often fatal to mankind. And it is all the more absurd to picture savages as continually cutting one another's throats to indulge their brutality, because this opinion is directly contrary to experience. The Caribs, who have so far departed least of all from the state of nature, are in fact the most peaceable people in their loves, and the least subject to jealousy, even though they live in a hot climate that always seems to inflame the passions.

As for the inferences that might be drawn from the case of several species of animals, the males of which fill our poultry yards with blood and slaughter, or in spring make the forests resound with their quarrels over their females, we must begin by excluding all those species in which nature has plainly established, in the comparative power of the sexes, relations different from those that exist among us. Thus we can base no conclusion about men on the habits of fighting cocks. In those species where the proportion is better observed, these battles must be due entirely to the scarcity of females compared with males—or, what comes to the same thing, to the intervals during which the female consistently refuses the male's advances. For if each female admits the male only during two months in the year, it is the same as if the number of females were five-sixths less. Now neither of these two cases applies to the human species, in which the number of females usually exceeds that of males, and where it has never been observed, even among savages, that the females have, like those of other animals, their fixed times of passion and indifference. Moreover, in several of these species, the individuals all catch fire at once, and there comes a fearful moment of universal passion, tumult, and disorder among them—a scene never seen in the human species, whose love is not seasonal. So we must not conclude, from the battles of such animals for the enjoyment of the females, that the case would be the same with mankind in a state of nature. And even if we drew such a conclusion, we see that such contests do not exterminate other kinds of animals, and we have no reason to think they would be more fatal to ours. It is, in fact, clear that they would do even less harm than is the case in a state of society—especially in those countries where, morals being still held in some repute, the jealousy of lovers and the vengeance of husbands daily cause duels, murders, and even worse crimes, where the obligation of eternal fidelity only produces adultery, and the very laws of honor and continence necessarily increase debauchery and multiply abortions.

Let us conclude, then, that man in a state of nature, wandering up and down the forests, without industry, without speech, and without home, an equal stranger to war and to all ties, neither needing his fellow creatures nor wanting to hurt them, and perhaps not even distinguishing them from one another—let us conclude that, being self-sufficient and subject to so few passions, he could have no feelings or knowledge but such as befitted his situation; that he felt only his actual needs, and disregarded everything he didn't think he was immediately concerned with, and that his understanding made no greater progress than his vanity. If by accident he made any discovery, he was all the less able to communicate it to others, since he didn't even know his own children. Every art would necessarily perish with its inventor, where there was no kind of education among men, and generations succeeded generations without the least advance. Setting out from the same point, centuries must have elapsed in the barbarism of the earliest ages; when the race was already old, man remained a child.

If I have lingered at such length on this supposed primitive state, it is because I had so many ancient errors and deep-rooted prejudices to uproot, and therefore thought it incumbent on me to dig down to their very roots and to show, by means of a true picture of the state of nature, how far even the natural inequalities of mankind are from having the reality and influence that modern writers suppose.

It is in fact easy to see that many of the differences distinguishing human beings are merely the effect of habit and of the different ways of life people adopt in society. Thus a robust or delicate constitution, and the strength or weakness it entails, are more often the effects of a hardy or soft education than of the body's original endowment. The same is true of the powers of the mind: education not only makes a difference between those who are cultivated and those who are not, but even increases the differences that exist among the former, in proportion to their respective degrees of cultivation—as the distance between a giant and a dwarf on the same road increases with every step they take. If we compare the prodigious diversity in the education and way of life of the various classes of men in the state of society with the uniformity and simplicity of animal and savage life, in which everyone lives on the same kind of food and in exactly the same manner, and does exactly the same things, it is easy to conceive how much less the difference between man and man must be in a state of nature than in a state of society, and how greatly the natural inequality of mankind must be magnified by the inequalities of social institutions.

But even if nature really did show, in the distribution of her gifts, that partiality which is attributed to her, what advantage would the greatest of her favorites derive from it, to the detriment of others, in a state that admits of hardly any kind of relation between them? Where there is no love, of what use is beauty? Of what use is wit to those who do not converse, or cunning to those who have no business with others? I hear it constantly repeated that, in such a state, the strong would oppress the weak. But what is meant here by oppression? Some, it is said, would violently lord it over others, who would groan under a servile submission to their whims. This indeed is exactly what I observe to be the case among us, but I don't see how it can be inferred about men in a state of nature, who could not easily be brought to grasp what we mean by dominion and servitude. One man, it is true, might seize the fruits another had gathered, the game he had killed, or the cave he had chosen for shelter. But how would he ever be able to exact obedience? And what ties of dependence could there be among men without possessions? If, for instance, I am driven from one tree, I can go to the next; if I am disturbed in one place, what prevents me from going to another? Again, if I should happen to meet a man so much stronger than myself, and at the same time so depraved, so lazy, and so barbarous as to compel me to provide his sustenance while he himself remains idle, he would have to take care never to take his eyes off me for a single moment; he would have to tie me up fast before going to sleep, or I would certainly either crack him on the head or make my escape. That is, he would have to voluntarily expose himself to much greater trouble than he is seeking to avoid, or could give me. After all that, let him be off his guard ever so little, let him just turn his head aside at any sudden noise, and I will be twenty paces off in an instant, lost in the forest; my fetters broken, he would never see me again.

Without wasting more time on these details, everyone must see that since the bonds of servitude are formed merely by the mutual dependence of men on one another and by the reciprocal needs that unite them, it is impossible to make any man a slave unless he is first reduced to a situation in which he cannot do without the help of others. And since such a situation does not exist in a state of nature, everyone there is his own master, and the law of the strongest has no effect.

Having proved that the inequality of mankind is hardly felt, and that its influence is next to nothing in a state of nature, I must next show its origin and trace its progress through the successive developments of the human mind. Having shown that human perfectibility, the social virtues, and the other faculties that natural man potentially possessed could never develop on their own but must require the fortuitous concurrence of many foreign causes that might never arise, and without which he would have remained forever in his primitive condition, I must now collect and consider the different accidents that may have improved the human understanding while corrupting the species, and made man wicked while making him sociable—so as to bring him and the world from that distant period to the point at which we now behold them.

I confess that, since the events I am going to describe might have happened in various ways, I have nothing to determine my choice but conjectures. But such conjectures become reasons when they are the most probable that can be drawn from the nature of things, and the only means of discovering the truth. The consequences I mean to deduce, however, will not be merely conjectural; for on the principles just laid down, it would be impossible to form any other theory that would not yield the same results, and from which I could not draw the same conclusions.

This will be a sufficient apology for my not dwelling on how the lapse of time compensates for the little probability of the events; on the surprising power of trivial causes when their action is constant; on the impossibility, on the one hand, of destroying certain hypotheses, though on the other we cannot give them the certainty of known matters of fact; on its being within the province of history, when two facts are given as real and have to be connected by a series of intermediate facts that are unknown or supposed to be so, to supply such facts as may connect them; and on its being in the province of philosophy, when history is silent, to determine similar facts to serve the same end; and lastly, on the influence of similarity, which, in the case of events, reduces the facts to a much smaller number of different classes than is commonly imagined. It is enough for me to offer these hints for my judges' consideration, and to have arranged things so that the general reader doesn't need to consider them at all.

chapters.title: Part 2
paragraphs: The true founder of civil society was the first man who fenced off a piece of land, thought of saying This is mine, and found people simple enough to believe him. How many crimes, wars, murders, horrors and misfortunes might someone have spared mankind by tearing out the stakes or filling in the ditch and calling to his fellows, "Beware of listening to this impostor; you are undone if you once forget that the fruits of the earth, belong to us all, and the earth itself to nobody." Yet things had very probably already reached a point at which they could no longer remain as they were. The idea of property depends on many earlier ideas, acquired one after another; it could not have appeared in the human mind all at once.

Human beings must already have advanced a great deal, acquiring considerable knowledge and practical skill, passing these on and enlarging them from age to age, before reaching this final stage of the state of nature. Let us therefore go further back and try to bring that slow sequence of events and discoveries into a single view, following their most natural order.

Man's earliest feeling was awareness of his own existence; his earliest concern was to preserve himself. The earth's produce supplied everything he needed, and instinct taught him to use it. Hunger and other appetites made him experience different ways of existing at different times. One of these urged him to reproduce his species--a blind impulse, unconnected with the heart, producing a purely animal act. Once the need was satisfied, the sexes had no further knowledge of one another. Even a mother's offspring meant nothing to her as soon as it could survive without her.

Such was man's infancy: an animal life confined at first to sensations, scarcely taking advantage of nature's gifts and still less able to conceive of wresting anything from her. But obstacles soon arose, and he had to learn to overcome them. Trees were too tall for him to gather their fruit; other animals competed for the same food; those that needed it to survive were fierce. All this forced him to develop his physical powers. He needed agility, speed and strength in fighting. Stones and sticks, nature's weapons, lay ready to hand. He learnt to overcome natural obstacles, fight other animals when necessary, and dispute the means of subsistence even with other men, or find compensation for what a stronger man forced him to surrender.

As mankind's numbers grew, so did its concerns. Differences of soil, climate and season must have produced differences in ways of life. Barren years, long bitter winters, and scorching summers that dried up the earth's fruits must have called forth new skills. People living along seashores and riverbanks invented hooks and lines, becoming fishermen and eating fish. In forests they made bows and arrows and became hunters and warriors. In cold regions they wore the skins of animals they had killed. Lightning, a volcano or some fortunate accident introduced them to fire, a new defence against winter's severity. They learnt first to keep it alive, then to produce it, and finally to cook animal flesh that they had previously eaten raw.

Repeated encounters with different beings, in relation both to himself and to one another, would naturally make man perceive certain relationships among them. The relations we call great, small, strong, weak, swift, slow, fearful, bold and so forth were compared almost unconsciously as need arose. Eventually these comparisons must have produced a kind of reflection--or rather a mechanical prudence--that showed him the precautions most necessary for his safety.

The intelligence developed in this way made him still more superior to other animals by making him aware of his superiority. He now tried to trap them and played a thousand tricks on them. Though many surpassed him in speed or strength, he gradually became master of some and a scourge to others. Thus his first inward glance brought his first feeling of pride. While he could still scarcely distinguish the different orders of beings, he ranked his species highest, preparing himself to claim superiority as an individual.

Other men admittedly did not then mean to him what they mean to us today. He associated with them no more than with other animals, but still included them in his observations. Over time he noticed similarities among them, and between himself and his female. These led him to infer further similarities he could not yet perceive. Seeing that they behaved as he would have behaved in comparable circumstances, he naturally concluded that their thinking and acting matched his own. Once this important truth had taken firm hold of his mind, an intuitive feeling, surer and much quicker than reasoning, must have guided him towards the conduct best suited to his own safety and advantage in dealing with them.

Experience taught him that the desire for well-being alone motivates human action. He could then distinguish the few occasions on which shared interests justified relying on his fellows' assistance, and the still fewer occasions on which conflicting interests gave him reason to distrust them. In the first case he joined their herd, or at most a loose association whose members remained unrestricted and whose existence ended with the passing need that had created it. In the second, each pursued his private advantage: openly by force if he felt strong enough, through skill and cunning if he felt weaker.

In this way men may gradually have gained rough ideas of mutual commitments and of the advantages to be gained by keeping them--but only where their immediate, obvious interests were involved. They knew nothing of foresight. Far from worrying about the distant future, they scarcely thought about tomorrow. When hunting a deer, everyone understood that success required him to stay faithfully at his post. Yet if a hare came within one hunter's reach, he would undoubtedly chase it without hesitation. Once he had caught his prey, he would care little that his companions might thereby lose theirs.

Clearly, such dealings needed language little more developed than that of rooks or monkeys, which gather for much the same purpose. For a long time inarticulate cries, abundant gestures and a few imitative sounds must have formed the universal language. Different countries then added conventional articulated sounds--whose original establishment, as I have already suggested, is not easy to explain--and particular languages emerged. But these were crude and incomplete, much like those still found among some savage nations.

Pressed by time's swift passage, by all I have to say, and by the almost imperceptible progress of things at their beginnings, I cross countless ages in an instant. The more slowly events followed one another, the more quickly their story can be told.

These early advances enabled further ones to follow more quickly. Growing knowledge brought greater practical skill. Men no longer slept beneath the first tree or in the first cave offering shelter. They invented various tools of hard, sharp stone for digging the earth and cutting wood. Next they built huts from branches, later learning to coat them with mud and clay. This was the first revolution: it established distinct families and introduced a kind of property, itself the source of a thousand disputes and conflicts. Probably the strongest were the first to build huts they felt able to defend. We may therefore suppose that weaker men found imitation easier and safer than trying to drive them out. Once a man possessed a hut, he had no reason to seize his neighbour's. This was less because it belonged to someone else than because it would be useless to him, and he could take it only by risking a desperate fight with the family living there.

The first unfolding of the human heart came from this new situation, bringing husbands and wives, fathers and children beneath one roof. Living together soon produced humanity's finest feelings: conjugal love and paternal affection. Each family became a small society, bound all the more closely because freedom and mutual attachment were its only ties. The sexes, whose lives had previously followed the same pattern, now adopted different ones. Women became more settled, tending the hut and children; men went out to seek food for them all. This gentler life cost both sexes some of their strength and fierceness. Yet although individuals became somewhat less able to face wild animals alone, they could more easily gather to resist them together.

Life in this new condition was simple and solitary. Man had few wants and tools to meet them, leaving him considerable leisure. He used it to provide comforts unknown to his fathers. This was the first yoke he unknowingly laid on himself, and the first source of the evils he prepared for his descendants. Besides further weakening body and mind, habitual use drained these comforts of almost all their pleasure. They even became actual needs, until doing without them was far more painful than possessing them had ever been pleasant. Losing them would make men unhappy, although having them no longer made them happy.

We can now see more clearly how speech became established and gradually improved within each family. We can also conjecture how various causes spread language and hastened its development by making it increasingly necessary. Floods or earthquakes surrounded inhabited regions with water or precipices. Upheavals of the globe tore land from continents and turned it into islands. Plainly, men gathered in this way and forced to live together would develop a common language much more readily than those still wandering through continental forests. It is therefore quite possible that islanders brought speech to the mainland after their first experiments in navigation. It is at least highly probable that communities and languages arose first on islands, and even reached perfection there before the mainland knew them.

Everything now begins to take on a different appearance. Men who had wandered through the woods adopt a more settled life, gradually draw together and form separate groups. Eventually each country has a distinct nation. Its character and customs are united, not by regulations or laws, but by similar food and ways of living and the shared effects of climate. Lasting proximity inevitably creates ties between families. Young men and women in neighbouring huts meet to satisfy nature's passing need; repeated contact soon produces another relationship, equally pleasant and more enduring. People begin to notice differences and make comparisons. Almost without knowing it, they acquire ideas of beauty and merit, which soon create preferences. Seeing one another often makes them unable to bear not seeing one another continually. A tender, agreeable feeling enters their hearts, but the slightest obstacle turns it into violent fury. Love brings jealousy; discord triumphs, and human blood is offered to the gentlest passion of all.

As new thoughts and feelings followed one another and both heart and mind came into play, men gradually shed their original wildness. Their personal ties grew closer each day as their circle widened. They began gathering around a great tree in front of their huts. Singing and dancing, the true children of love and leisure, became the amusement--or rather the occupation--of men and women assembled with nothing else to do. Everyone began to look at others and wanted to be looked at in return. Public esteem thus acquired value. The best singer or dancer, the most handsome, strong, skilful or eloquent person won the most regard. This marked the first step towards both inequality and vice. These earliest distinctions produced vanity and contempt on one side, shame and envy on the other. Fermenting together, these new ingredients eventually formed combinations fatal to innocence and happiness.

Once people began assessing one another, and the idea of esteem took root in their minds, everyone claimed a share of it. It could no longer be denied to anyone without consequences. Thus even savages acquired the first duties of civility. Every deliberate injury became an insult: besides the damage itself, the injured person was sure to see contempt for his person, often harder to bear than the harm.

Each man punished others' contempt according to his own opinion of himself. Revenge therefore became terrible, and men grew cruel and bloodthirsty. This is precisely the condition reached by most savage nations we know. Failing to distinguish our ideas properly, and to recognise how far these peoples already stand from the state of nature, many writers have hastily declared man naturally cruel and in need of civil institutions to soften him. Yet nothing is gentler than man in his original condition. Nature places him midway between the stupidity of beasts and civilised man's disastrous ingenuity. Instinct and reason alike confine him to protecting himself from threatening harms. Natural compassion restrains him from injuring others, and he is not prompted to injure them even in retaliation. For, as the wise Locke's axiom says, There can be no injury, where there is no property.

We must observe, however, that the society now formed and the relationships now established among men demanded qualities different from those they had possessed in their original constitution. Morality began entering human actions. Before laws existed, each person alone judged and avenged injuries done to him. The goodness suited to the pure state of nature no longer fitted society's infancy. More frequent opportunities to offend required harsher punishments, and fear of revenge had to replace the severity of law. Men had thus become less patient and their natural compassion had already weakened. Nevertheless, this age, in which human faculties expanded, must have been the happiest and most stable. It held a proper balance between the original condition's idleness and our egoism's restless activity. Reflection increasingly shows that this was the condition least exposed to revolutions and altogether the best man could experience. Only some fatal accident could have driven him from it--an accident that, for the common good, should never have occurred. Most savages have been found in this condition. Their example seems to show that men were meant to stay there, that this was the world's true youth, and that every later advance apparently perfected the individual while actually carrying the species towards decrepitude.

As long as men were happy with their rustic huts; as long as clothing made from animal skins, sewn with thorns and fish-bones, was enough; as long as their ornaments were only feathers and shells, and their activities were painting their bodies in different colours, improving and decorating bows and arrows, or using sharp stones to make fishing boats and crude musical instruments--in short, as long as they attempted only what one person could do, and practised arts needing no shared labour--they lived freely, healthily, honestly and happily for as long as their nature permitted, enjoying independent yet mutual companionship. But once one man needed another's help, once someone saw an advantage in storing enough food for two, equality vanished. Property appeared, labour became essential, and vast forests turned into smiling fields. Men watered those fields with the sweat of their brows, and slavery and misery soon sprouted and grew alongside the crops.

The two arts responsible for this great revolution were metallurgy and agriculture. Poets blame gold and silver; philosophers see iron and corn as the things that first civilised men and ruined humanity. Neither of these arts was known to the savages of America, who consequently remain savage. Other nations likewise seem to have stayed barbarous while practising only one. Perhaps one of the strongest explanations for Europe's more continuous and advanced civilisation--if not its greater antiquity--is that Europe has both the richest supplies of iron and the most fertile cornlands.

How men first discovered and used iron is hard to imagine. They could hardly have thought on their own of mining ore and preparing it for smelting before knowing what the result would be. Nor is an accidental fire a likely explanation. Mines occur only in barren places without trees or plants, as though nature had taken care to conceal this fatal secret from us. That leaves only the extraordinary chance of a volcano throwing out molten metal and suggesting to onlookers that they imitate nature's operation. We must further suppose that these men possessed unusual courage and foresight to attempt such laborious work with so remote a prospect of benefit. Yet those qualities occur together only in minds more developed than we can suppose the first discoverers' minds to have been.

Agriculture's principles, by contrast, were understood long before they were practised. Men who constantly drew their food from plants and trees could scarcely fail to learn readily how nature reproduced them. Yet probably a very long time passed before their efforts turned to cultivation. Trees, together with hunting and fishing, already fed them without needing attention. Or perhaps they did not know how to use corn, or lacked tools to grow it; perhaps they did not anticipate future needs; or, finally, perhaps they had no means of stopping others from stealing the fruits of their labour.

As their practical skills developed, they probably began growing a few vegetables or roots near their huts, using sharp stones and pointed sticks. But a long time passed before they learnt to prepare corn or acquired the tools needed to raise it in substantial quantities. Agriculture also demands willingness to accept an immediate loss for a future gain. Such foresight was alien to the savage mind: as I have said, a savage scarcely anticipates in the morning what he will need that night.

The invention of other arts must therefore have been needed to drive mankind towards agriculture. Once craftsmen were required to smelt and forge iron, other people had to provide the food that maintained them. Manufacturing employed more and more hands, leaving fewer available to supply everyone's subsistence, while the number of mouths needing food remained unchanged. Some people needed commodities in return for their iron; the others eventually discovered how iron could increase the supply of commodities. Thus husbandry and agriculture became established on one side, and metalworking with its multiplying uses on the other.

Cultivating the earth necessarily led to dividing it. Once property was recognised, the first rules of justice followed: before each man could be secured in what was his, each had to be able to possess something. Moreover, men now looked ahead and all had something to lose. Each therefore had reason to fear retaliation for injuries done to others. This origin is especially natural because property can scarcely be conceived as arising from anything but manual labour. What else can a man add to things he did not originally create to make them his own? The farmer's labour alone gives him a right to his crops and, with it, a claim to the soil he has cultivated, at least until harvest. Renewed year after year, this becomes continuous possession, readily transformed into property. According to Grotius, when the ancients called Ceres Legislatrix and named a festival in her honour Thesmophoria, they meant that dividing the land had produced a new right: property, distinct from the right derived from the law of nature.

Equality might have survived in this situation if individuals had possessed equal abilities and, for instance, iron use and the consumption of commodities had always balanced exactly. But nothing maintained that balance, and it soon broke down. The strongest man did the most work; the most skilful made best use of his labour; the most inventive found ways to reduce it. The farmer needed more iron, or the smith more corn. Though both worked equally hard, one profited greatly while the other barely survived. Natural inequality thus gradually develops alongside the inequality created by association. Differences among men, enlarged by their differing circumstances, become more visible and lasting in their effects, and increasingly determine each individual's lot.

Once matters reached this stage, the rest is easy to imagine. I shall not delay the reader with accounts of the successive invention of other arts, the growth of language, the testing and use of talents, unequal fortunes, the use and abuse of wealth, and all the related details he can readily supply himself. I shall merely glance at mankind in this new condition.

Look now at human faculties fully developed: memory and imagination freely at work, egoism engaged, reason active, and the mind approaching its highest perfection. See every natural quality operating, each man's rank and condition determined--not only by his property and ability to help or harm others, but by wit, beauty, strength, skill, merit or talents. Since only these qualities could command respect, people soon had either to possess them or to pretend they did.

Men now benefited from appearing to be what they were not. Being and seeming became entirely separate, and from their separation came arrogant display, deceitful cunning and the many vices accompanying them. Once free and independent, men were now burdened with so many new wants that they became dependent, as it were, on all nature, and especially on one another. Even a man who mastered others became in some measure a slave. The rich needed others' services, the poor their help; those between could not do without others either. Man therefore had to spend his life persuading people to take an interest in his fate, and making them see at least an apparent advantage, if not a real one, in advancing his interests. Towards some he had to be sly and calculating, towards others domineering and cruel. He was almost compelled to mistreat those he needed whenever he could neither frighten them into obedience nor see a benefit in serving them. Boundless ambition and the thirst for greater fortunes--arising less from actual need than from wanting to surpass others--filled everyone with a base inclination to harm his fellows. They also inspired secret jealousy, all the more dangerous for hiding behind benevolence to achieve its aims more safely. In short, rivalry and competition arose on one side, conflicting interests on the other, and on both a concealed wish to gain at others' expense. These were property's first evils, inseparable companions of growing inequality.

Before symbols representing wealth were invented, riches could consist scarcely of anything except land and cattle, the only real possessions men can have. But once estates multiplied and expanded until they occupied all the land and bordered one another, a man could enlarge his holdings only at someone else's expense. Meanwhile those left over, too weak or idle to acquire holdings, had become poor without losing anything: everything around them changed while they stayed the same. They had to obtain their food from the rich or steal it from them. Depending on their characters, domination and slavery followed, or violence and plunder. The rich, once they tasted the pleasure of command, despised every other pleasure. Using old slaves to acquire new ones, they thought only of subduing and enslaving their neighbours. They resembled ravenous wolves that, after tasting human flesh once, reject every other food and seek only men to devour.

The most powerful and the most destitute alike treated their strength or misery as a right to others' possessions, equal in their eyes to the right of property. Equality's destruction therefore brought terrible disorder. The rich seized, the poor robbed, and both let their passions run unchecked. Natural compassion's cries and justice's still-faint voice were silenced, while greed, ambition and vice filled men's hearts. The strongest man's claim and the first occupier's claim clashed endlessly, with nothing but battle and bloodshed to settle them. Society's infancy thus produced a dreadful state of war. Tormented and corrupted, men could no longer turn back or surrender their fatal acquisitions. Abusing the very faculties that honoured them, they worked only towards their own undoing and brought themselves to the edge of ruin.
Attonitus novitate mali, divesque miserque, Effugere optat opes; et quæ modô voverat odit.[5]

Men must eventually have reflected on this miserable condition and the disasters overwhelming them. The rich especially must have felt the cost of constant war, whose entire expense fell on them. Everyone risked life, but they alone risked property. However plausibly they disguised their seizures, they knew their claims were false and insecure. If others forcibly took what they themselves had gained by force, they had no grounds for complaint. Even men enriched by their own labour could hardly claim a better title. They might repeat in vain, "I built this well; I gained this spot by my industry." Someone could answer: who gave you your position? What right have you to ask us to pay for work we never requested? Do you not know that many fellow-creatures starve for lack of what you possess in excess? Before taking more of the common food supply than your own maintenance required, you should have obtained mankind's explicit, universal consent. The rich man had no sound justification and insufficient strength to defend himself. He could easily crush individuals, yet a band of robbers could easily crush him. He stood alone against everyone. Mutual jealousy prevented him from joining his equals against numerous enemies united by hope of plunder. Driven by necessity, he finally conceived the deepest plan ever to enter a human mind: to turn his attackers' strength to his own advantage, make allies of his enemies, teach them different principles, and give them institutions as favourable to him as the law of nature was unfavourable.

With this aim he first described to his neighbours the horrors of their situation: every man armed against the rest, possessions as burdensome as wants, and no security in either wealth or poverty. He then easily devised persuasive arguments to win them over. "Let us join," said he, "to guard the weak from oppression, to restrain the ambitious, and secure to every man the possession of what belongs to him: let us institute rules of justice and peace, to which all without exception may be obliged to conform; rules that may in some measure make amends for the caprices of fortune, by subjecting equally the powerful and the weak to the observance of reciprocal obligations. Let us, in a word, instead of turning our forces against ourselves, collect them in a supreme power which may govern us by wise laws, protect and defend all the members of the association, repulse their common enemies, and maintain eternal harmony among us."

Far fewer words of this kind would have deceived men so barbarous and easily persuaded. Their disputes were too numerous for them to manage without arbitrators, and their ambition and greed too great for them to remain long without masters. Everyone rushed towards chains, hoping to secure freedom. They had enough understanding to see political institutions' advantages, but too little experience to foresee their dangers. Those best able to anticipate the dangers were precisely those expecting to profit from them. Even the most prudent thought it wise to surrender part of their freedom to protect the remainder, just as a wounded man has an arm amputated to save his body.

Such was, or may well have been, the birth of society and law. These fastened new chains on the poor and bestowed new powers on the rich. They destroyed natural liberty beyond recovery, fixed property and inequality for ever, and turned skilful usurpation into unalterable right. For a few ambitious individuals' benefit, they condemned mankind to endless labour, slavery and misery. One community's establishment plainly made others necessary: to resist united forces, everyone else had to unite as well. Societies soon multiplied across the earth until hardly any corner remained where a man could escape the yoke and withdraw from the sword he saw forever hanging above him by a thread. Civil right now governed relations within each community. The law of nature survived only between communities, where, renamed the right of nations, it was modified by tacit agreements to allow commerce. These agreements also replaced natural compassion, which lost almost all its influence when applied to societies rather than individuals. It survived only in a few great cosmopolitan souls who broke through the imaginary barriers between peoples. Following our Sovereign Creator's example, they extended their benevolence to the whole human race.

But political bodies remained in a state of nature towards one another and soon suffered the difficulties that had driven individuals out of it. For these great bodies, that condition proved still more deadly than for the individuals composing them. Hence came national wars, battles, murders and reprisals, shocking nature and outraging reason, together with the dreadful prejudices that count the honour of shedding human blood among the virtues. The most distinguished men learnt to regard cutting one another's throats as a duty. Eventually men slaughtered their fellows by the thousand without even knowing why. A single day's battle brought more murders, a single town's sack more violent outrages, than entire ages of the state of nature across the whole earth. These were the first observable consequences of dividing mankind into separate communities. But let us return to their institutions.

I know some writers offer different accounts of the origin of political societies, through conquest by the strong or through association among the weak. Which of these causes we choose does not, in fact, affect my argument. Still, the explanation I have just given seems the most natural to me, for the following reasons. First, conquest creates no right in itself and therefore cannot provide a foundation for any other right. Conqueror and conquered remain at war unless the defeated people, restored to complete freedom, voluntarily choose the victor as their chief. Until then, any terms of surrender rest on force and are therefore ipso facto void. On this account there could be no real society or body politic, and no law except the strongest man's. Second, in the alternative explanation, strong and weak are ambiguous. During the interval between the establishment of property or prior occupancy and the institution of political government, rich and poor express their meaning better. Before laws existed, men could subject their equals only by attacking their possessions or transferring some of their own to them. Third, the poor had nothing left to lose except freedom. It would have been utterly absurd to surrender voluntarily the only good they still enjoyed and receive nothing whatever in exchange. The rich, however, had feelings, if I may put it this way, in every part of their property. They were much easier to hurt, and therefore had greater need to protect themselves. In short, it is more reasonable to suppose an institution invented by those who would benefit from it than by those whom it must injure.

Government initially had no settled, regular form. Without experience or philosophy, men saw only immediate difficulties and thought of preventing others only after they arose. Despite the wisest legislators' efforts, the political state stayed imperfect because it was largely the product of chance. Having begun badly, it never repaired its original faults, even when time exposed them and suggested remedies. People continually patched it up. To build something stable and lasting, they should first have cleared the site and removed the old materials, as Lycurgus did at Sparta. At first society consisted merely of a few general agreements that every member promised to observe. The whole body guaranteed to each individual that these promises would be kept. Only experience could reveal how weak this constitution was and how easily people could violate it without punishment. Conviction was difficult when the public alone served as both witness and judge. Laws were inevitably evaded in countless ways, while disorder and inconvenience multiplied. Eventually public authority had to be dangerously entrusted to private persons, and a magistrate charged with enforcing the people's decisions. To suggest that chiefs were chosen before the association existed, or that administrators of laws preceded the laws themselves, is too absurd to take seriously.

It would be equally unreasonable to suppose that men immediately surrendered themselves, unconditionally and beyond recall, to an absolute master. Could proud, unconquered men really have chosen a headlong plunge into slavery as their first means of common protection? Why appoint superiors at all, unless to defend them from oppression and protect their lives, liberties and property--the elements, so to speak, of their existence? In relations between individuals, nothing is worse than being at another's mercy. Common-sense therefore forbids supposing that men began by giving a chief the very things they wanted him to preserve. What could he offer in return for so enormous a right? If he dared demand it as the price of protection, would they not answer in the fable's words, "What more can the enemy do to us?" It is therefore indisputable, and indeed the basic principle of all political right, that peoples appointed chiefs to protect their liberty, not enslave them. If we have a prince, said Pliny to Trajan, it is to save ourselves from having a master.

Politicians reason as falsely about love of liberty as philosophers do about the state of nature. They use what they have seen to judge very different things they have never seen. Because the slaves they observe bear their yoke patiently, they attribute a natural inclination to servitude to mankind. They forget that liberty resembles innocence and virtue: only those possessing them know their worth, and losing them also destroys the taste for them. "I know the charms of your country," said Brasidas to a Satrap, who was comparing life at Sparta with life at Persepolis, "but you cannot know the pleasures of mine."

An untamed horse raises its mane, paws the earth and recoils violently at the sight of a bridle; a trained horse patiently endures whip and spur. So the savage refuses to bend his neck beneath a yoke that civilised man accepts without protest, preferring the most troubled freedom to the most peaceful slavery. We therefore cannot infer mankind's natural attitude towards slavery from the submissiveness of peoples already enslaved. We must look instead at the immense efforts every free people makes to resist oppression. I know enslaved nations endlessly praise the tranquillity of their chains and call miserable servitude peace: miserrimam servitutem pacem appellant.[6] But I see free peoples sacrificing pleasure, peace, wealth, power and life itself for that one treasure which those who have lost it despise. I see free-born animals dash their brains against cage bars because they cannot naturally endure captivity. I see naked savages, contemptuous of European pleasures, face hunger, fire, swords and death simply to preserve their independence. Then I feel that slaves are not the people to reason about liberty.

Some writers derive absolute government and all society from paternal authority. Without repeating the opposing arguments of Locke and Sidney, it is enough to observe how utterly unlike despotism's ferocious spirit this gentle authority is. It looks more to the benefit of the person obeying than to the benefit of the person commanding. Under the law of nature, a father rules his child only while the child needs his help. Afterwards they are equals; the son is entirely independent and owes respect, not obedience. Gratitude is a duty to fulfil, not a right to enforce. Instead of deriving civil society from paternal authority, we should say that paternal authority draws its chief strength from civil society. No individual was recognised as father of many until his sons and daughters stayed settled around him. His possessions, which he truly controls, are the ties keeping his children dependent. If he chooses, he can deny them any share unless they earn it through constant deference to his wishes. An arbitrary despot's subjects, however, can expect no comparable favour from their ruler. They and everything they own belong to him, or so he considers them. They must therefore accept as a favour the little of their own that he chooses to leave them. Stripping them of their possessions counts as justice; allowing them to live counts as mercy.

Testing facts against right in this way would reveal as little reason as truth in the notion that tyranny was voluntarily established. It would also be hard to justify a contract binding only one party, placing all risk on that side and none on the other, so that only the person bound could suffer. Even in modern times this hateful system is far from the practice of wise, good monarchs, especially France's kings. Several passages in their edicts show this, notably the following words from a celebrated edict issued in 1667 in the name and by order of Louis XIV.

"Let no one therefore claim that the Sovereign stands outside the laws of his State. The opposite is a true principle of the right of nations. Flattery has sometimes challenged it, but good princes have always defended it as the protecting divinity of their realms. How much more justly we may say, with the wise Plato, that a kingdom's perfect happiness lies in subjects obeying their prince, the prince obeying the laws, and those laws being just and always directed towards the public good!"[7]

I shall not pause to ask whether renouncing liberty, man's noblest faculty, degrades our very nature and lowers us to beasts enslaved by instinct. Nor shall I ask whether surrendering the most precious of His gifts without reservation affronts the Author of our being, forcing us to commit crimes He forbids simply to please a mad or cruel master; or whether this sublime craftsman should be less angered by the complete destruction of His work than by its dishonour. If my opponents wish, I will set aside Barbeyrac's authority. Following Locke, he declares firmly that no man can sell his freedom so completely as to submit to an arbitrary power free to use him however it wishes. For, he adds, this would mean selling his own life, which he does not own. I ask only what right those willing to degrade themselves in this way could have to inflict the same disgrace on their descendants. How could they renounce for them blessings that do not come from their ancestors' generosity, and without which life burdens everyone worthy of living it?

Puffendorf says we may surrender liberty to other men just as contracts and agreements transfer property from one person to another. This seems a very weak argument. First, property I give away becomes wholly separate from me, and its misuse cannot harm me. The misuse of my liberty, however, concerns me intimately. If I expose myself to becoming an instrument of crime, I cannot avoid guilt for the crimes I may be forced to commit. Moreover, property rights rest only on conventions made by men, so men may dispose of their possessions as they choose. Essential gifts of nature, such as life and liberty, are different. Everyone is allowed to enjoy them, and it is at least doubtful that anyone has a right to surrender them. Giving up liberty degrades our being; giving up life does all it can to extinguish it. No worldly benefit can compensate for either loss, so renouncing either at any price offends both reason and nature. Even if liberty could be transferred like property, children would remain a very different case. They receive their father's estate only through the transfer of his right. Their liberty, however, comes from nature because they are human beings, and their parents have no right whatever to take it away. Establishing slavery thus required violence against nature; perpetuating such a right would require changing nature itself. Jurists who solemnly declare a slave's child born a slave have effectively ruled that a man shall enter the world without being a man.

I therefore take it as certain that government did not originate in arbitrary power. Such power is government's corruption and final extreme, returning it at last to the law of the strongest that it was meant to remedy. Even supposing government had begun this way, power illegitimate in itself could not have founded society's laws, or consequently the inequality those laws established.

Further investigation is still needed into the nature of the fundamental compact underlying every government. Without undertaking those inquiries here, I shall accept the common view of it: the political body begins with a genuine contract between the people and the chiefs they have chosen. Both parties undertake to observe the laws stated in that contract, which form the bonds of their union. For their social relations the people combine all their wills into one. The separate articles expressing this will become fundamental laws binding every State member without exception. One article governs the selection and powers of magistrates charged with enforcing the others. Their authority includes everything that preserves the constitution, but nothing that changes it. Honours accompany it so that laws and their administrators command respect. Personal privileges also distinguish these ministers, compensating them for the labour and care that sound administration demands. The magistrate, for his part, promises to exercise his entrusted power only according to his constituents' intentions, to keep everyone in peaceful possession of what is theirs, and always to place the public interest before his own.

Before experience revealed this constitution's inevitable abuses, or knowledge of the human heart allowed men to foresee them, it must have seemed all the more excellent because those charged with preserving it had the strongest interest in doing so. Magistracy and its rights rested entirely on the fundamental laws. If those laws disappeared, the magistrates' legitimacy would disappear too, and the people would owe them no further obedience. Since laws, not magistrates, are essential to a State's existence, its members would then recover their right to natural liberty.

Even slight reflection supplies further arguments confirming this truth and convinces us that the contract cannot, by its very nature, be irrevocable. If no higher power could guarantee the parties' faithfulness or compel them to honour their mutual commitments, each would judge his own case. Each would retain the right to withdraw as soon as the other broke the terms, or those terms ceased to suit him. This principle may provide the basis for a right of abdication. In considering this institution here, we are concerned only with what is human in its nature and establishment. If the magistrate, holding all power and appropriating every advantage of the contract, still has a right to surrender his authority, the people must have a much stronger right to end their dependence, since they suffer for every fault of their chief. Yet such a dangerous privilege would necessarily produce countless terrible disputes and disorders. These show above all how badly human governments needed a firmer foundation than reason alone. For public peace, it was expedient that the divine will should intervene, investing sovereign authority with a sacred, inviolable character and depriving subjects of the fatal right to dispose of it. Even had religion given the world no other benefit, this would oblige men to accept and cultivate it despite its abuses: it has saved more blood than fanaticism has ever shed. But let us return to the course of our hypothesis.

Different forms of government arose from the different degrees of inequality existing among individuals when governments were founded. If one man stood out in power, virtue, wealth or personal influence, he became sole magistrate and the State a monarchy. If several men of roughly equal standing rose above the rest, they were elected together and formed an aristocracy. Where a people had moved less far from the state of nature, and differences of wealth or talent were smaller, supreme administration remained shared and democracy resulted. Time revealed which forms suited men best. Some peoples remained entirely under the laws; others soon obeyed magistrates instead. Citizens worked to preserve their liberty. Subjects, angered by seeing others enjoy a blessing they had lost, thought only of enslaving their neighbours. In short, wealth and conquest developed on one side, happiness and virtue on the other.

All offices in these different governments were originally elective. When wealth did not influence the choice, preference went to merit, which gives natural authority, and to age, which brings practical experience and considered counsel. The Hebrew Elders, Sparta's Gerontes, Rome's Senate, and the very origin of our word Seigneur show the reverence once paid to old age. Yet choosing older men meant more frequent elections, making the process increasingly troublesome. Intrigues developed, factions formed, partisan feeling turned bitter, and civil wars erupted. Individual lives were sacrificed to the State's supposed happiness, until men nearly fell back into their original anarchy. Ambitious chiefs exploited these circumstances to keep their offices permanently within their own families. Meanwhile the people, accustomed to dependence, ease and life's comforts, and no longer able to break their chains, accepted deeper slavery for the sake of tranquillity. Once magistracy became hereditary, its holders grew used to treating office as a family estate and themselves as owners of communities they had originally only served. They regarded fellow-citizens as slaves, counted them among their possessions like cattle, and called themselves the gods' equals and kings of kings.

Following inequality's progress through these successive revolutions, we find its first stage in the establishment of laws and property rights, its second in the institution of magistracy, and its third and last in the conversion of legitimate power into arbitrary power. The first period authorised the condition of rich and poor; the second, that of powerful and weak; only the third, that of masters and slaves. This last distinction is inequality's final degree. All the others remain there once they reach it, until further revolutions either dissolve government altogether or restore its legitimacy.

To see why this development is necessary, we should look less at the motives for founding the body politic than at its actual forms and inevitable defects. The same human failings that require social institutions make their abuse unavoidable. Sparta is an exception: its laws chiefly concerned children's education, and Lycurgus established morals that virtually removed the need for laws. Usually, laws are weaker than passions and restrain men without changing them. Apart from Sparta, it would be easy to show that a government scrupulously fulfilling its founding purposes and carefully guarding against corruption and change had been established needlessly. A country where nobody evaded laws or misused magisterial power would need neither laws nor magistrates.

Political distinctions inevitably produce distinctions in civil life. The growing inequality between chiefs and people soon affects individuals, taking a thousand forms according to passions, talents and circumstances. A magistrate cannot seize unlawful power without raising the dependants with whom he must share it. Individuals, moreover, submit to oppression only as blind ambition drives them onward. Looking below rather than above themselves, they learn to love authority more than independence and accept slavery so that they can enslave others in turn. A man without any wish to command is hard to force into obedience. Even the cleverest politician could not enslave a people whose only wish was independence. But inequality readily penetrates cowardly, ambitious minds, always willing to gamble with fortune and almost indifferent to commanding or obeying as fortune favours or opposes them. There must therefore have been a time when the people's sight was so bewitched that a ruler needed only to tell the lowest man, "Be great, you and all your posterity," for everyone, including the man himself, immediately to see greatness in him. His descendants assumed still more importance the further removed they were from him. The dimmer and less certain the cause, the greater its effect: a family became more illustrious as the number of idlers it could count increased.

If this were the place for detail, I could readily explain why, even without government intervention, unequal standing and authority became inevitable among individuals. Once joined in one society, they compared themselves and noticed differences revealed by their necessary, continual dealings with neighbours.[8] Those differences take several forms. Wealth, nobility or rank, power and personal merit are the chief distinctions by which people assess one another socially. I could prove that agreement or conflict among these forces provides the surest sign of a State's good or bad constitution. I could show that although personal qualities originally produce the other inequalities, wealth eventually absorbs all four. Riches most directly advance individual prosperity and are easiest to transfer, so they purchase every other distinction. This observation lets us judge fairly precisely how far a people has left its original constitution behind and how close it has come to corruption's ultimate extreme. I could explain how the universal desire for reputation, honours and advancement, burning in us all, exercises our powers and faculties and sets them against one another. It stimulates and multiplies passions; it creates competition and rivalry--or rather hostility--everywhere. By sending so many aspirants along the same course, it brings innumerable failures, successes and disturbances of every kind. I could show that the longing to be talked about and the relentless passion to distinguish ourselves produce both our best and worst possessions: virtues and vices, knowledge and errors, conquerors and philosophers--in other words, many bad things and very few good. Finally, I could prove why a handful of rich and powerful men occupy fortune's and grandeur's summit while the multitude crawls in poverty and obscurity. The former value what they have only because others lack it. Without any alteration in their own circumstances, they would stop being happy the moment the people stopped being miserable.

These details alone would provide enough material for a substantial work. It could weigh every kind of government's advantages and disadvantages in relation to man in the state of nature. It could also show the different forms inequality has taken so far or may take in future ages, according to the nature of governments and the changes time must inevitably bring. We would then see multitudes oppressed from within by the very precautions they had taken against foreign tyranny. We would see oppression steadily advance, while its victims could discover neither where it might stop nor what lawful means remained for resisting it. Citizens' rights and nations' freedom would slowly die out; the weak's complaints, protests and appeals would be dismissed as seditious murmuring. Political calculation would reserve the honour of defending the common cause for a mercenary section of the people. Taxes would become necessary as a result. Discouraged farmers would abandon their fields even in peacetime, leaving the plough to strap on a sword. Fatal, arbitrary codes of honour would arise. Sooner or later the country's defenders would become its enemies, forever holding daggers against their fellow-citizens' breasts. Eventually they would address their country's oppressor in the following words.
Pectore si fratris gladium juguloque parentis Condere me jubeas, gravidæque in viscera partu Conjugis, invitâ peragam tamen omnia dextrâ. Lucan. i, 376.

Great inequalities of wealth and condition, the immense variety of passions and talents, useless and harmful arts, and empty sciences would produce countless prejudices equally opposed to reason, happiness and virtue. We would see magistrates encourage anything that weakened people joined in society by setting them against one another. They would foster anything that sowed real division while preserving an appearance of harmony, and anything that inspired mutual hatred and distrust between ranks by opposing their rights and interests. In this way they would strengthen the power standing over them all.

Amid this disorder and these revolutions, despotism would slowly raise its hideous head, devouring everything still sound and uncorrupted in every part of the State. At last it would trample laws and people alike and settle on the republic's ruins. Trouble and disaster would mark the period just before this final transformation.
