Eventually, however, the monster would swallow everything. The people would have neither chiefs nor laws, only tyrants. From then on virtue and morality would have no place. Despotism, cui ex honesto nulla est spes, recognises no other master wherever it rules. The moment it speaks, honesty and duty lose their force, and blind obedience becomes the only virtue slaves can still practise.

This is inequality's final stage, the farthest point that closes the circle and rejoins the point from which we began. All private individuals return to their original equality because they count for nothing. Subjects know no law except their master's will; their master knows no restraint except his passions. Every notion of goodness and principle of justice vanishes again. The law of the strongest returns completely, bringing a new state of nature. Unlike the original state in its first purity, this one results from excessive corruption. In other respects the two conditions differ so little, and despotism dissolves the governmental contract so thoroughly, that the despot rules only while he remains strongest. Once he can be driven out, he has no right to complain of force. A popular uprising that kills or deposes a Sultan is as lawful as the acts by which he disposed of his subjects' lives and fortunes the previous day. Force alone sustained him; force alone removes him. Everything thus follows the natural order. Whatever these frequent, sudden revolutions produce, no man has grounds to accuse another of injustice, but only to blame his own bad luck or imprudence.

If the reader discovers and retraces this lost, forgotten path by which man must have moved from the state of nature into society, he cannot fail to be struck by the immense distance between them. He must carefully reconstruct not only the intermediate conditions I have described, but those lack of time forced me to omit or imagination failed to suggest. Following this slow sequence will resolve many political and moral problems that philosophers cannot settle. He will understand that men differ from age to age: Diogenes could not find a man because he sought among his contemporaries a man belonging to an earlier time. He will see why Cato died with Rome and liberty: he was unsuited to his age. That greatest of men could only astonish a world he would certainly have governed had he lived five hundred years earlier. In short, the reader will explain how men's souls and passions gradually change their very nature, why their needs and pleasures eventually seek different objects, and why original man has slowly disappeared. Society now presents only artificial men and manufactured passions, produced by these new relationships without any true foundation in nature. Everything reflection teaches on this subject is fully confirmed by observation. Savage and civilised man differ so deeply in their hearts and inclinations that one's greatest happiness would plunge the other into despair. The savage breathes only peace and liberty. He wants simply to live without labour. Even the Stoic's ataraxia falls far short of his profound indifference to everything else. Civilised man, meanwhile, constantly moves, sweats, works and strains his mind to discover still more demanding occupations. He drudges until his last moment, even seeking death to put himself in a position to live, or giving up life to gain immortality. He courts powerful men he hates and wealthy men he despises, stopping at nothing for the honour of serving them. Without shame he prides himself on his own baseness and their protection. Proud of his slavery, he scorns those who lack the honour of sharing it. What a spectacle a European minister of State's bewildering, envied labours would offer a Caribean! How many cruel deaths this idle savage would prefer to such a horrible life, seldom sweetened even by the pleasure of doing good! To understand the motives behind all this anxious effort, however, he would need to attach meaning to the words power and reputation. He would need to know that some men value the world's opinion, finding happiness and self-satisfaction in others' testimony rather than their own. The true source of these differences is that the savage lives within himself, whereas social man continually lives outside himself. He knows how to live only in others' opinions, seeming to derive awareness of his very existence from their judgment of him. My purpose here is not to dwell on the resulting indifference to good and evil, despite our many fine moral writings. Nor is it to show how, once everything becomes appearance, honour, friendship, virtue and often even vice itself become mere contrivance and masquerade, and we eventually learn to boast even of vice. Nor need I show how, always asking others what we are and never daring to ask ourselves, we possess, amid so much philosophy, humanity, civilisation and sublime morality, only a frivolous, deceptive appearance: honour without virtue, reason without wisdom, pleasure without happiness. It is enough to have proved that this is in no way man's original condition. Society's spirit and the inequality it produces are what transform and distort all our natural inclinations.

I have tried to follow inequality's origin and development, and political societies' establishment and abuse, as far as reason alone can deduce them from human nature, independently of the sacred doctrines that give sovereign authority the sanction of divine right. This examination shows, first, that inequality scarcely exists in the state of nature. The inequality now prevailing therefore gains its growth and strength from the development of our faculties and the progress of the human mind, finally becoming lasting and legitimate through property and law. Second, moral inequality authorised solely by positive right conflicts with natural right whenever it does not correspond to physical inequality. This distinction sufficiently determines our judgment of the inequality found in every civilised country. However the law of nature is defined, it plainly contradicts it for children to command old men, fools to command the wise, or a privileged few to gorge on excess while the starving multitude lacks life's bare necessities.
